_schema.notes: CS extension pack over the core ontology. Units (learnable, with retrieval states): topic, mechanism, algorithm, architecture, component. Capsules (binary understood): failure, tradeoff, pattern, paper + core insight/question. Hubs: concept. Dependency edges (requires/builds_on) define the curriculum order; causal edges (causes/solves/optimizes) encode reasoning; fails_when/trades encode engineering judgment; instance_of links topics to recurring engineering patterns; described_in links to primary sources. Every entity may carry `why` — the first-principles reason it exists.

entities.en: how information becomes computable
the next-token objective
how models get good
the transformer
serving tokens fast
prompting & context engineering
beyond the model
evaluation, cost, reliability
splitting text into subword units
entities.why: Models cannot consume raw strings; they need a finite vocabulary of discrete symbols. Subwords balance vocabulary size against sequence length.
entities.ex: Before anything else happens, Tokenization turns the prompt into a sequence of integer ids.
entities.xt: It is the first stage of every forward pass — and the source of many odd behaviors (counting letters, arithmetic).

entities.en: the atomic unit of model input · a subword id
entities.why: Characters are too slow, words are too many. Subword tokens are the compromise every modern LLM uses.
entities.ex: A Token is roughly three quarters of an English word on average.
entities.xt: Pricing, context limits and speed are all measured in tokens.

entities.en: mapping discrete symbols to dense vectors of meaning
entities.why: Neural networks compute with continuous numbers, not symbols. Embeddings place meaning in a geometry where similarity becomes distance.
entities.ex: An Embedding turns token 4091 into a 4096-dimensional vector whose neighbors mean similar things.
entities.xt: The same trick powers recommenders, search, vision and RAG — it is a universal representation strategy.

entities.en: the geometry where meaning lives
entities.why: Once meaning is geometric, reasoning about similarity becomes linear algebra: directions, distances, projections.
entities.ex: In the model's Vector space, 'king' minus 'man' plus 'woman' lands near 'queen'.
entities.xt: Semantic arithmetic is evidence that directions encode features.

entities.en: multiply-and-sum similarity of two vectors
entities.why: It is the cheapest possible question one vector can ask another: how much do you point my way? Attention scores and retrieval both reduce to it.
entities.ex: Every attention score starts life as a Dot product between a query and a key.
entities.xt: One primitive, billions of times per token.

entities.en: angle-based similarity of two vectors
entities.why: Raw dot products grow with vector length; dividing it out leaves pure direction — meaning without magnitude.
entities.ex: Vector search ranks chunks by Cosine similarity to the query embedding.
entities.xt: The workhorse metric of every vector database.

entities.en: assigning probabilities to sequences of text
entities.why: If you can score any continuation, you can generate, complete, translate and reason — one objective subsumes hundreds of tasks.
entities.ex: Language modeling reduces every text task to one question: how likely is this continuation?
entities.xt: The unreasonable effectiveness of one objective.

entities.en: predicting the next token given all previous ones
entities.why: Text provides its own labels: every position is a training example. Self-supervision at internet scale is what made LLMs possible.
entities.ex: Next-token prediction gives the model a training signal at every single position for free.
entities.xt: No human labels needed — the corpus supervises itself.

entities.en: scores over the whole vocabulary that sum to 1
entities.why: The model never answers with one token — it answers with beliefs over all of them. Everything downstream (sampling, loss, calibration) operates on this object.
entities.ex: Each forward pass ends in a Probability distribution over every token in the vocabulary.
entities.xt: Generation is repeated sampling from these beliefs.

entities.en: the uncertainty of a distribution in bits
entities.why: Compression and prediction are the same problem: a model that predicts well is a model that compresses well. Entropy is the currency of both.
entities.ex: High Entropy in the output distribution means the model genuinely does not know what comes next.
entities.xt: Watching it per-token is a cheap hallucination detector.

entities.en: how surprised a model is by the true data
entities.why: Training needs a number that says how wrong the belief was. Cross-entropy charges the model log-loss for the probability it failed to put on the truth.
entities.ex: Pretraining minimizes Cross-entropy between predicted distributions and actual next tokens.
entities.xt: Perplexity is just its exponential.

entities.en: the single number training tries to minimize
entities.why: Optimization needs a scalar target. Compressing 'how wrong were we' into one differentiable number is what makes gradient descent applicable at all.
entities.ex: Every gradient in the network flows backward from one scalar Loss.
entities.xt: Change the loss and you change what the model becomes.

entities.en: raw unnormalized scores before softmax
entities.why: The network's last layer produces free-range real numbers; probabilities need normalization. Logits are the honest raw opinion before it.
entities.ex: The final linear layer maps the hidden state to Logits, one per vocabulary token.
entities.xt: Logprobs APIs expose (log of) what these become after softmax.

entities.en: turning raw scores into a probability distribution
entities.why: You need all scores comparable, positive, and summing to one — while keeping ranking and being differentiable. Exponentiate-then-normalize is the canonical answer.
entities.ex: Softmax exponentiates each logit and divides by the sum, giving a valid distribution.
entities.xt: Used twice per layer: in attention weights and at the output head.

entities.en: choosing the next token from the distribution
entities.why: Always taking the argmax makes output repetitive and brittle; drawing from the distribution injects controlled variation. Decoding strategy is a product decision, not a detail.
entities.ex: Greedy decoding, temperature and top-p are all variants of Sampling from the same distribution.
entities.xt: The same model can feel deterministic or creative purely through this knob.

entities.en: a knob that sharpens or flattens the distribution
entities.why: Dividing logits by T rescales confidence: T→0 approaches argmax, T>1 flattens toward uniform. One scalar controls the explore/exploit dial of generation.
entities.ex: Raising the Temperature flattens the distribution, so rarer tokens get sampled more often.
entities.xt: Named after the Boltzmann distribution in statistical physics.

entities.en: sampling only from the smallest set covering p probability
sy: sampling from the top probability mass
entities.why: Temperature alone still leaves an infinite junk tail. Top-p cuts the tail adaptively: wide when the model is uncertain, narrow when it is sure.
entities.ex: With Top-p at 0.9, tokens outside the top 90% of probability mass can never be sampled.
entities.xt: Usually combined with temperature, and often confused with it.

entities.en: stacked learnable matrix transforms with nonlinearities
sy: layers of weighted sums and nonlinearities
entities.why: You need a function family expressive enough to represent language and differentiable enough to train. Deep stacks of linear maps plus nonlinearities are that family.
entities.ex: A Neural network is just matrix multiplies and nonlinearities, repeated until intelligence falls out.
entities.xt: The transformer is one specific wiring of this idea.

entities.en: computing every gradient via the chain rule
entities.why: Training needs the gradient of one loss with respect to billions of weights. Reverse-mode autodiff gets all of them in one backward pass at the cost of roughly one forward pass.
entities.ex: Backpropagation reuses intermediate activations to compute all gradients in a single backward sweep.
entities.xt: Dynamic programming applied to calculus.

entities.en: iteratively stepping weights downhill on the loss
sy: iterative weight updates against the gradient
entities.why: The loss surface has billions of dimensions and no closed form. Local slope is the only signal available at scale — so follow it, in minibatches, with momentum.
entities.ex: Gradient descent nudges every weight a small step against its gradient, millions of times.
entities.xt: Adam, SGD, RMSProp — all variations on this loop.

entities.en: forward, loss, backward, update — repeated at scale
entities.why: All of pretraining is one four-beat loop distributed over thousands of GPUs. Understanding it demystifies every training curve you will ever read.
entities.ex: The Training loop runs forward, computes loss, backpropagates, and updates — then does it again, trillions of times.
entities.xt: Everything else in ML infrastructure exists to keep this loop fed and stable.

entities.en: loss falls predictably with compute, data and parameters
entities.why: They turned model building from alchemy into budgeting: given a compute budget, the optimal model size and data mix are calculable before training.
entities.ex: Scaling laws predicted that a smaller model trained on more tokens would beat a larger undertrained one.
entities.xt: Chinchilla's core insight — and why data became the bottleneck.

entities.en: continuing training on task-specific data
sy: adapting a pretrained model with more training
entities.why: Pretraining buys general competence; a few thousand curated examples buy behavior. Cheaper than pretraining, more permanent than prompting.
entities.ex: Fine-tuning changes the weights themselves, so the behavior persists without any prompt.
entities.xt: Use it for style and format; use retrieval for facts.

entities.en: aligning outputs with human preferences via reward models
sy: training against a learned reward model
entities.why: Cross-entropy rewards imitating the internet; humans want helpful, honest, harmless. RLHF swaps the objective: optimize what people prefer, as scored by a learned reward model.
entities.ex: RLHF is why chat models refuse, hedge, and apologize — the reward model taught them to.
entities.xt: The step that turned raw LLMs into assistants.

entities.en: training a small model to mimic a large one
sy: small model mimicking a large one
compressing a model into a smaller one
entities.why: The big model's full output distribution is a far richer teacher than one-hot labels. Capability compresses better than it trains from scratch.
entities.ex: Distillation trains the student on the teacher's soft probabilities, not just the right answer.
entities.xt: How flagship quality reaches phone-sized models.

entities.en: processing sequences one step at a time with hidden state
entities.why: The first serious answer to variable-length input: carry a summary forward. Its failure — a single bottleneck state and no parallelism — is why attention exists.
entities.ex: An RNN must squeeze the entire past through one fixed-size hidden state.
entities.xt: Know it to explain why the transformer won.

entities.en: an RNN with gates that protect long-range memory
entities.why: Vanishing gradients erased long-range signal in RNNs; gates gave gradients a protected highway. It stretched recurrence a decade further before attention replaced it.
entities.ex: The LSTM's gates decide what to keep, what to forget, and what to output at each step.
entities.xt: State of the art for NLP until roughly 2017.

entities.en: every token directly weighting every other token
entities.why: Recurrence forced information through a serial bottleneck. Attention removes it: any token can query any other directly, and all pairs compute in parallel on GPUs.
entities.ex: Attention lets 'it' look directly at 'the animal' fifty tokens back and decide they refer to the same thing.
entities.xt: A differentiable, soft version of a hash-table lookup.

entities.en: the three projections that implement attention
entities.why: A lookup needs three roles: what I seek (Q), what I advertise (K), what I hand over (V). Learning three separate projections lets one token play all roles at once.
entities.ex: Each token emits a Query · Key · Value triple; scores are Q·K, outputs are score-weighted V.
entities.xt: The database analogy is exact — select values where keys match the query, softly.

entities.en: several attention lookups running in parallel subspaces
entities.why: One head averages all relationships into mush. Splitting into subspaces lets one head track syntax, another coreference, another position — simultaneously.
entities.ex: Multi-head attention runs 32 small lookups in parallel and concatenates what they find.
entities.xt: Interpretability work finds heads with recognizable jobs.

entities.en: injecting token order into an order-blind mechanism
entities.why: Attention is a set operation — permute the input and outputs permute too. Language is not a set, so order must be injected explicitly.
entities.ex: Without Positional encoding, 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would be indistinguishable.
entities.xt: Modern models use rotary embeddings (RoPE) for this.

entities.en: adding each layer's input to its output
entities.why: Hundred-layer gradients die crossing hundred transformations. Residuals give both signal and gradient an identity highway; layers learn small refinements instead of full rewrites.
entities.ex: A Residual connection means each layer computes a correction, not a replacement.
entities.xt: The single trick that made very deep networks trainable.

entities.en: normalizing activations to keep training stable
entities.why: Deep stacks drift: activations explode or collapse across layers. Re-centering and re-scaling at every layer keeps every depth in a trainable regime.
entities.ex: LayerNorm rescales each token's activation vector to zero mean and unit variance before the sublayer.
entities.xt: Boring, invisible, and load-bearing.

entities.en: the per-token MLP where most parameters live
entities.why: Attention moves information between tokens; the FFN transforms it per token. Roughly two thirds of parameters sit here — much of the model's stored knowledge.
entities.ex: After attention mixes context, the Feed-forward network processes each token independently.
entities.xt: Current evidence: facts are largely stored in these weights.

entities.en: stacked attention + FFN blocks — the LLM architecture
entities.why: Take attention, wrap it with residuals and norms for trainability, add FFNs for capacity, positions for order — and stack. Every frontier model is this recipe scaled.
entities.ex: A Transformer is the same block — attention, FFN, residuals, norms — repeated dozens of times.
entities.xt: GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama: one architecture, different scale and data.

entities.en: storing past keys and values to avoid recomputation
entities.why: Autoregressive decoding revisits the same past every step. Cache each token's K and V once, and generation cost per token drops from quadratic to linear.
entities.ex: The KV cache is why generating token 1000 does not require reprocessing tokens 1–999.
entities.xt: Its memory footprint — not compute — is what limits concurrent users per GPU.

entities.en: exact attention computed IO-aware in fast memory
entities.why: Attention was bottlenecked by memory traffic, not math: writing the N×N matrix to slow GPU memory. Tiling the computation to stay in SRAM removes that traffic — exactly, not approximately.
entities.ex: FlashAttention never materializes the full attention matrix, computing it tile by tile in on-chip memory.
entities.xt: A lesson in profiling: the bottleneck was bandwidth, not FLOPs.

entities.en: a small model drafts, the big model verifies in parallel
sy: small model drafts big model verifies
entities.why: Big-model forward passes are the cost center, but verifying k tokens costs one pass while generating them costs k. Let a cheap drafter propose and the big model check — output provably identical.
entities.ex: Speculative decoding accepts several drafted tokens per large-model pass, often 2–3× faster.
entities.xt: Free lunch bought with an accept/reject sampling proof.

entities.en: packing many requests into each GPU pass
sy: serving many requests per forward pass
packing requests together on the gpu
entities.why: One request cannot saturate a GPU built for parallelism. Interleaving many requests — admitting and retiring them mid-flight — is where serving economics are won.
entities.ex: Continuous batching slots new requests into the batch the moment any sequence finishes.
entities.xt: The core scheduling idea inside vLLM and friends.

entities.en: emitting tokens to the client as they are generated
entities.why: Total generation takes seconds; the first token takes tens of milliseconds. Shipping tokens as they exist converts dead wait into perceived responsiveness.
entities.ex: Streaming does not make the model faster — it makes the wait visible and therefore bearable.
entities.xt: Time-to-first-token became a headline metric because of this.

entities.en: storing weights in fewer bits
sy: compressing weights to int8 or int4
entities.why: Weights are trained in 16-bit but tolerate 8 or 4 bits with minor loss. Halving bits halves memory and doubles bandwidth-bound speed — the cheapest 2× in inference.
entities.ex: Quantization to 4 bits lets a 70B model fit where a 16-bit 20B model did.
entities.xt: Outlier channels are the reason naive rounding fails — see LLM.int8().

entities.en: time to first token and time per token
entities.why: LLM latency has two independent components — prefill (context processing) and decode (per token) — and every optimization targets one or the other. Conflating them leads to wrong fixes.
entities.ex: Prefill dominates Latency for long prompts; decode speed dominates for long answers.
entities.xt: Diagnose which one hurts before reaching for a fix.

entities.en: programming the model through its input text
entities.why: A next-token predictor continues patterns; whoever writes the context controls the pattern. Prompting is programming where the source code is the input.
entities.ex: Prompting works because the model continues whatever document you make it believe it is writing.
entities.xt: The cheapest, fastest, least permanent way to change behavior.

entities.en: standing instructions with elevated priority
entities.why: Products need behavior users cannot casually override. A privileged instruction channel, reinforced by training, separates the operator's voice from the user's.
entities.ex: The System prompt sets persona, rules and tools before the user says a word.
entities.xt: Its authority comes from RLHF training, not from magic.

entities.en: teaching the task by showing examples in context
entities.why: The model learned to continue patterns; examples define a pattern more precisely than instructions describe it. Show, don't tell — no weight updates required.
entities.ex: Three Few-shot examples of the output format beat a paragraph describing it.
entities.xt: In-context learning was GPT-3's headline discovery.

entities.en: making the model reason step by step before answering
entities.why: Each token gets a fixed compute budget; hard problems need more. Intermediate reasoning tokens are extra computation the model buys itself, with each step conditioning the next.
entities.ex: Chain of thought trades more tokens for more serial computation on the problem.
entities.xt: Reasoning models made this an explicit, trained-for phase.

entities.en: the maximum tokens the model can attend over
entities.why: Attention is all-pairs, so context costs quadratic compute and linear KV memory — a real physical budget. Everything the model 'knows right now' must fit inside it.
entities.ex: Anything outside the Context window does not exist for the model — there is no other memory.
entities.xt: Context engineering is deciding what deserves those tokens.

entities.en: constraining generation to a schema like JSON
entities.why: Software needs parseable data, and 99% valid JSON is 0% parseable. Masking invalid tokens during sampling makes conformance a guarantee instead of a request.
entities.ex: Structured output masks every token that would violate the schema before sampling.
entities.xt: Constrained decoding turns prose engines into API endpoints.

entities.en: the model emitting typed calls your code executes
entities.why: Models cannot act — they can only emit text. Structured call-intents that your runtime executes and answers close the loop between language and the world.
entities.ex: In Function calling the model outputs {name, arguments}; your code runs it and returns the result.
entities.xt: The model proposes; the runtime disposes.

entities.en: retrieving relevant knowledge into the context before generating
entities.why: Weights are frozen, stale and expensive to change; documents are live and cheap. Fetch what is relevant now and let the model read instead of remember.
entities.ex: RAG swaps 'know everything' for 'know where to look' — retrieval plus reading.
entities.xt: The default architecture for private-knowledge products.

entities.en: splitting documents into retrievable pieces
entities.why: Whole documents embed into mush and overflow context; sentences lose their surroundings. Chunk size sets the resolution of everything retrieval can find.
entities.ex: Bad Chunking can split an answer across two chunks so neither gets retrieved.
entities.xt: The most underrated knob in every RAG pipeline.

entities.en: an index for fast nearest-neighbor search over embeddings
entities.why: Exact search over millions of vectors is too slow per query. ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF) trade a sliver of recall for orders-of-magnitude speed.
entities.ex: A Vector database answers 'which chunks are nearest this query embedding' in milliseconds.
entities.xt: The same separation of storage and compute as any database.

entities.en: finding the most relevant chunks for a query
entities.why: Generation quality is capped by context quality: the model cannot cite what retrieval did not fetch. Most 'model failures' in RAG are retrieval failures.
entities.ex: Retrieval quality caps RAG quality — garbage fetched, garbage generated.
entities.xt: Debug the retrieved set before blaming the model.

entities.en: re-scoring candidates with a stronger relevance model
entities.why: Fast retrieval casts a wide, sloppy net. A cross-encoder that reads query and chunk together is slow but precise — run it on only the top 50.
entities.ex: Reranking reads each candidate with the query jointly, catching relevance the embeddings missed.
entities.xt: Cheap-filter-then-expensive-verify, the classic two-stage design.

entities.en: combining keyword and semantic retrieval
entities.why: Embeddings blur exact identifiers (error codes, names); keyword search cannot see paraphrase. Fuse both rankings and each covers the other's blind spot.
entities.ex: Hybrid search finds 'ERR_CONN_RESET' by keyword even when its embedding is unremarkable.
entities.xt: Reciprocal rank fusion is the usual glue.

entities.en: a model in a loop: observe, decide, act with tools
entities.why: One shot cannot handle tasks that need investigation and course correction. Put the model in a loop where each action's result informs the next decision.
entities.ex: Agents chain model turns and tool results until the goal is reached or abandoned.
entities.xt: Reliability compounds per step — an anti-scaling law to engineer against.

entities.en: extending the model with external capabilities
entities.why: Search, code execution and databases are better at facts, math and state than any set of weights. Delegate what tools do better; keep the model for judgment.
entities.ex: Tool use lets the model run the query instead of hallucinating its result.
entities.xt: Choosing what stays in the model vs. moves to tools is an architecture decision.

entities.en: decomposing a goal into ordered, checkable steps
entities.why: Long-horizon tasks fail step by step unless the horizon is made explicit. A stated plan is inspectable, checkable and revisable — silent improvisation is none of these.
entities.ex: Planning first, then executing step by step, beats improvising on every hard multi-step task.
entities.xt: Also what makes agent behavior auditable.

entities.en: measuring model quality systematically
entities.why: Outputs are open-ended, so quality has no exit code. Without evals, every prompt change is a blind bet; with them, iteration becomes engineering.
entities.ex: Evaluation suites turn 'it feels better' into a number you can regress against.
entities.xt: The single highest-leverage practice in LLM product work.

entities.en: shared public tests of model capability
entities.why: Comparison needs common ground, so the field standardizes tests — which then leak into training data and saturate. Trust them directionally, never absolutely.
entities.ex: Benchmarks saturate and contaminate; your own eval on your own task is the ground truth.
entities.xt: Goodhart's law, applied at industry scale.

entities.en: watching quality, cost and safety in production
entities.why: Offline evals sample yesterday's distribution; users sample today's. Drift, regressions and abuse only show up if you are watching live traffic.
entities.ex: Monitoring catches the prompt regression your offline eval suite never covered.
entities.xt: Logging model traffic is step zero of every LLM ops story.

entities.en: tokens × price, at prefill and decode rates
entities.why: Every architectural choice — context length, caching, model tier, retries — is secretly a cost decision. Teams that cannot attribute cost per feature cannot optimize it.
entities.ex: Cost scales with tokens processed, so context bloat is a billing problem before it is a quality problem.
entities.xt: Prompt caching and small-model routing are the two big levers.

entities.en: confident, fluent, wrong
entities.body: The model states falsehoods with the same fluency as truths. Root cause: the training objective rewards plausible continuation, not verified fact — truth and plausibility usually correlate, until they don't.
entities.why: Not a bug in one model but a property of the objective. Mitigate with grounding (RAG), tools, calibration and evals — not by asking nicely.

entities.en: data that hijacks instructions
entities.body: Untrusted content — a web page, an email, a retrieved chunk — contains text that the model treats as instructions. Instructions and data share one channel: the context.
entities.why: The LLM analogue of SQL injection, but with no reliable escaping. Defense in depth: privilege separation, tool allowlists, human confirmation on side effects.

entities.en: all-pairs scoring scales O(n²)
entities.body: Every token attends to every other token, so doubling context quadruples attention compute. Long contexts get expensive faster than intuition suggests.
entities.why: The direct price of attention's power. FlashAttention optimizes the constant; sparse/linear attention and retrieval attack the asymptotics.

entities.en: mid-context information gets ignored
entities.body: Models retrieve information best from the start and end of a long context; facts buried in the middle are disproportionately missed — even when the context nominally 'fits'.
entities.why: A long context window is not uniform memory. Put critical instructions first or last, and don't equate fits-in-context with will-be-used.

entities.en: the right chunk never reaches the model
entities.body: The answer exists in the corpus but retrieval fetches the wrong chunks — bad chunk boundaries, vocabulary mismatch, or embedding blind spots. The model then improvises from nothing.
entities.why: The dominant failure mode of RAG systems in practice. Always inspect the retrieved set before blaming generation.

entities.en: the whole past squeezed through one state
entities.body: RNNs compress the entire history into a single fixed-size hidden vector, processed strictly in order. Long-range information fades, and training cannot parallelize across the sequence.
entities.why: The failure that motivated attention. Understanding it makes the transformer's design feel inevitable rather than arbitrary.

entities.en: spend RAM to avoid recomputation
entities.body: Caching K/V states, larger batches, longer contexts — all buy speed or throughput by consuming GPU memory, the scarcest resource on the card.
entities.why: The oldest tradeoff in computing, wearing a GPU costume. Serving capacity is usually memory-bound, not compute-bound.

entities.en: variance is both feature and bug
entities.body: Higher temperature and looser top-p produce fresher, more varied text — and more factual drift and format breakage. Tight sampling is reliable and dull.
entities.why: Pick per use case: extraction wants temperature 0; brainstorming wants variance. There is no universally correct setting.

entities.en: quality costs time and compute
entities.body: Bigger models, longer reasoning chains, reranking passes and verification steps all raise quality and response time together.
entities.why: Route by stakes: cheap-fast models for easy traffic, escalate hard cases. Uniform maximum quality is uniform maximum cost.

entities.en: every token in context is billed compute
entities.body: More context — examples, documents, history — improves grounding while inflating prefill cost quadratically and cache memory linearly. Stuffing context is paying for tokens the model may ignore.
entities.why: Context is a budget to allocate, not a bin to fill. Retrieval exists precisely to spend it well.

entities.en: one user's speed vs. everyone's volume
entities.body: Large batches maximize GPU utilization and tokens-per-second across users while making each individual response slower to start.
entities.why: The core dial of every serving system. Interactive products cap batch delay; offline pipelines max it out.

entities.en: store results instead of recomputing them
entities.body: KV caches, prompt caching, memoization, CPU caches, CDN edges, database indexes — the same move everywhere: pay memory once, save compute forever after.
entities.why: When the same subproblem recurs, the fastest computation is the one you never repeat. Recognizing this pattern lets you predict optimizations before reading the docs.

entities.en: a cheap proxy plus verification beats exact brute force
entities.body: Speculative decoding, quantization, ANN search, sampling itself: compute a cheap approximation, optionally verify with the expensive exact method only where it matters.
entities.why: Most of the cost of exactness buys precision nobody needed. Engineering is deciding where 'close enough' is.

entities.en: smaller representations that preserve what matters
entities.body: Embeddings compress meaning, distillation compresses capability, summarization compresses context, quantization compresses weights. Prediction and compression are formally the same task.
entities.why: Whatever survives compression is what the system considered essential — compression choices are modeling choices.

entities.en: keep knowledge outside the processor of it
entities.body: RAG keeps facts in a store and reasoning in the model, exactly as databases keep data out of application servers and KV caches keep state out of the attention loop.
entities.why: Storage and compute scale, update and fail differently. Coupling them means retraining to fix a typo.

entities.en: encode the goal as a number, then push on it
entities.body: Gradient descent, RLHF reward models, eval-driven prompt iteration, even A/B tests: define a measurable objective and iterate against it. The objective, not the intention, is what gets optimized.
entities.why: Systems Goodhart on whatever you actually measure. Choosing the objective is the highest-leverage — and most dangerous — decision.

entities.en: Vaswani et al., 2017
entities.body: Dropped recurrence entirely, keeping only attention plus feed-forward blocks. Trained faster, parallelized fully, and became the substrate of every modern LLM.
entities.why: Read it to see how few ingredients the architecture actually has — the paper is 11 pages and the recipe hasn't fundamentally changed since.

entities.en: Dao et al., 2022
entities.body: Showed attention was memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound, and reorganized the computation into SRAM-sized tiles for exact results with far less memory traffic.
entities.why: The canonical example of hardware-aware algorithm design in the LLM era — profile first, then restructure for the memory hierarchy.

entities.en: Hoffmann et al., 2022 — 'Chinchilla'
entities.body: Showed most large models were badly undertrained: for a fixed compute budget, parameters and training tokens should scale together (~20 tokens per parameter).
entities.why: Turned 'how big should the model be' from taste into arithmetic, and shifted the bottleneck from parameters to data.

entities.en: Brown et al., 2020 — GPT-3
entities.body: Demonstrated that a large enough language model performs new tasks from examples in the prompt alone — no fine-tuning, no gradient updates.
entities.why: The discovery of in-context learning: scale bought a new capability class, and prompting became an interface.

entities.q: Why does every AI course start with embeddings?
entities.body: Before any learning or reasoning, information must be shaped so a computer can act on it. Tokens then vectors is the LLM answer; pixels then features is vision's; rows then indexes is the database answer. Get the representation right and downstream problems soften.

entities.q: What problem was attention actually solving?
entities.body: RNNs forced the whole past through one fixed-size hidden state, serially. That meant forgetting at distance and no parallel training. Attention deleted the bottleneck — direct access between all positions — and the serial constraint, unlocking GPU-scale training. The transformer is what remains when you keep only that.

entities.q: What does turning temperature up actually cause?
entities.body: Temperature flattens the output distribution → rarer tokens get sampled → outputs are more diverse and creative → and more often unmoored from facts. Creativity and hallucination sit on the same dial; there is no setting that maximizes one without feeding the other.

entities.q: Where have you seen the KV cache pattern before?
entities.body: Dynamic programming, CPU caches, Redis, CDN edges, database indexes — all store computed results because recomputation is dearer than memory. Recognize the pattern and you can predict both the benefit and the cost model (memory pressure) without reading a line of vLLM.

entities.w: Embeddings are not an NLP trick
entities.q: Why do embeddings keep appearing outside NLP?
entities.body: Any similarity structure — products, songs, faces, code, proteins — can be embedded into a geometry where distance means relatedness. LLMs use them at the input layer; RAG uses them for search; recommenders used them first. One idea, a dozen industries.

entities.w: Why not just average all previous tokens?
entities.en: the classic attention interview question
entities.body: Averaging weights every past token equally — 'the' counts as much as the subject you need. Attention computes content-dependent weights per query: each token decides what matters to it, differently at every position and head. Averaging is attention with all weights frozen to 1/n.

entities.w: Why does the KV cache make decoding fast?
entities.en: the standard inference interview question
entities.body: Without it, generating token n reprocesses all n−1 previous tokens through every layer — O(n²) work over a generation. With cached K/V, each new token computes only its own projections and attends to stored state: O(n) overall, at the price of GPU memory that scales with context × layers × heads.

entities.en: separates users from engineers in one question
entities.body: It divides the logits before softmax. T<1 sharpens the distribution toward the argmax; T>1 flattens it toward uniform; T=0 is greedy decoding. It does not add 'randomness' — sampling was already random; it reshapes which outcomes carry probability mass.

entities.w: Your RAG answer is wrong — debug it
entities.en: the systems-thinking RAG interview question
entities.body: Bisect the pipeline: (1) Was the right chunk retrieved? If not — chunking, embeddings, hybrid search, reranking. (2) If retrieved, did the model use it? If not — context position, prompt framing, conflict with parametric memory. Most teams blame the model; most bugs live in retrieval.
